title: Pentose Phosphate Pathway & Uronic Pathway
objectives: Understand the two phases of the pentose phosphate pathway and their products
Explain the biological significance of NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate
Describe the regulation of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Recognize clinical implications of PPP enzyme deficiencies
Understand the role of the uronic acid pathway in detoxification

overview.title: Pathway Overview
overview.content:
Pentose Phosphate Pathway Overview

The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) is an alternative glucose metabolism pathway that produces ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant protection.

Key Features

  • Substrate: Glucose-6-phosphate
  • Primary products: Ribose-5-P (nucleotides) and NADPH (biosynthesis)
  • End products: Fructose-6-P and glyceraldehyde-3-P
  • Location: Cytosol of specific tissues

Tissue Distribution

Rapidly Dividing Cells

Tissues: Bone marrow, skin, intestinal mucosa, tumors

Requirement: Ribose-5-P for DNA/RNA synthesis

Lipogenic/Steroidogenic Tissues

Tissues: Liver, adipose, mammary glands, adrenal glands, gonads

Requirement: NADPH for fatty acid/steroid synthesis

pathway.title: Pathway Reactions
pathway.content:
PPP Reactions

Oxidative Phase (Irreversible)

1. Glucose-6-P Dehydrogenase

Reaction: Glucose-6-P → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH

Regulation: Rate-limiting, inhibited by NADPH/NADP+ ratio

2. 6-Phosphogluconate Dehydrogenase

Reaction: 6-phosphogluconate → ribulose-5-P + CO2 + NADPH

Non-oxidative Phase (Reversible)

3. Transketolase

Reaction: Transfers 2-carbon units (requires TPP)

Products: Sedoheptulose-7-P + glyceraldehyde-3-P

4. Transaldolase

Reaction: Transfers 3-carbon dihydroxyacetone moiety

Products: Fructose-6-P + erythrose-4-P

Net Outcome

3 Glucose-6-P → 3 CO2 + 6 NADPH + 2 Fructose-6-P + 1 Glyceraldehyde-3-P

regulation.title: Regulation
regulation.content:
PPP Regulation

Primary Control Points

G6PD: Committed step inhibited by high NADPH/NADP+ ratio

Hormonal: Induced by insulin in fed state

Substrate: Activated by glucose-6-P availability

Comparison with Glycolysis

Electron Acceptors: PPP uses NADP+, glycolysis uses NAD+

Energy: Glycolysis produces ATP, PPP does not

CO2: Released in PPP, not in glycolysis

clinical.title: Clinical Notes
clinical.content:
Clinical Correlations

G6PD Deficiency

Pathophysiology:

X-linked disorder causing impaired NADPH production, leading to oxidative damage in RBCs

Symptoms:

  • Hemolytic anemia and jaundice (neonatal or drug-induced)
  • Renal failure in severe cases
  • Triggered by infections, certain drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides), fava beans

Variants:

Mediterranean and Afro-Caribbean variants confer malaria resistance

Transketolase Deficiency

Association:

Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in thiamine deficiency (common in alcoholism)

Symptoms:

Memory loss, mental confusion, partial paralysis

uronic.title: Uronic Acid Pathway
uronic.content:
Uronic Acid Pathway

Alternative glucose pathway producing glucuronic acid for detoxification and proteoglycan synthesis.

Key Reactions

1. UDP-Glucose Dehydrogenase

Reaction: UDP-glucose → UDP-glucuronate (NAD+-dependent)

Function: Source of glucuronate for conjugation reactions

2. End Products

Primary: D-xylulose (enters PPP)

Functions: Proteoglycan synthesis, detoxification (bilirubin, drugs)

Clinical Aspects

Essential Pentosuria

Cause: L-xylulose reductase deficiency (benign)

Diagnosis: Positive urine reducing sugar test

Alimentary Pentosuria

Cause: Excessive fruit consumption (pears)

Note: Temporary and harmless

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Why can't erythrocytes use glycolysis instead of PPP for NADPH?
Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and depend entirely on PPP for NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione and protect against oxidative damage.
How does G6PD deficiency protect against malaria?
The heterozygous state creates an oxidative environment less favorable for malaria parasite survival in RBCs, providing selective advantage.
What's the clinical significance of UDP-glucuronate?
It conjugates bilirubin, steroid hormones, and drugs (like morphine) making them more water-soluble for excretion.
